267.title: Islam: one God
267.hook: the declaration of faith: there is no god but God, and Muhammad is God's messenger (Quran 112)
267.howItsDone: Muslims say the shahada in every daily prayer and hear it in every call to prayer; many whisper the call to prayer to a newborn and hope to say the shahada as their last words.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Lent, and ashes on the forehead. Your line was forty days. Today, a new visit: Islam.

A baby is born in a hospital in Cairo, or Jakarta, or Birmingham, Alabama. Within minutes, in many Muslim families, a father or grandfather leans close to the newborn's ear and softly speaks the call to prayer. So among the first words that baby ever hears is a sentence about God. And at the other end of life, families gathered at a bedside hope the same sentence will be among the last words spoken. First breath to last, one sentence frames it all: the shahada.
screen: `A NEWBORN, A WHISPER IN THE EAR.` → `A BEDSIDE, THE LAST WORDS.` → `THE SHAHADA.`

segments.voice: Shahada means witness, or testimony. It's the declaration at the heart of Islam, naming God and the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him: la ilaha illa Allah, Muhammad rasul Allah. There is no god but God, and Muhammad is the messenger of God. Allah is simply the Arabic word for God; Arab Christians use it too. The first half is about God: that God is one, with no partner and no rival. Muslims call this oneness tawhid, and it's the center of everything else. The second half is about the Prophet: that he is God's messenger, bringing the Qur'an. Saying the shahada sincerely, with understanding, is how a person becomes Muslim. It's the first of the five pillars of Islam, repeated in every call to prayer, five times a day, from minarets around the world. The Qur'an puts God's oneness most memorably in one of its shortest chapters, surah one hundred twelve. In Marmaduke Pickthall's 1930 translation: "Say: He is Allah, the One! Allah, the eternally Besought of all! He begetteth not nor was begotten. And there is none comparable unto Him." Four short lines. In Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet is reported to have said this little chapter equals a third of the Qur'an, and many Muslims recite it every day. Notice the shape: first a negation, no god, then an affirmation, but God. Many Muslim teachers say the negation clears the ground, all the false centers a life can have, money, status, fear, and the affirmation leaves only one.

segments.voice: Breathe in, and let the mind be as busy as it is; breathe out, and quietly say, one. Each time a thought pulls at you, a worry, a plan, a craving, notice it, and come back: one. If you're Muslim, you might hold the shahada itself; if not, let one be the only word in the room.
Shahada. Witness: there is no god but God, and Muhammad is the messenger of God. The first pillar of Islam. Today's word.

268.title: Islam: five prayers
268.hook: Muslims pray five times a day, facing Mecca
268.howItsDone: Muslims pray salat five times a day at set times, after washing with wudu and facing the Kaaba in Mecca, alone or together; on Fridays the midday prayer is held in congregation at the mosque.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the shahada, there is no god but God. Your line was one.

Pings, buzzes, banners: a phone's interruptions pull toward something someone else wants. Salat is an interruption of another kind. Five times, from before dawn to after dark, a Muslim who keeps the prayers stops what they're doing, washes, turns in one direction, and prays toward God. And because the times follow the sun, as dawn and dusk move across the time zones, a wave of prayer rolls around the planet all day. Today: salat, the five daily prayers.
screen: `PINGS, BUZZES, BANNERS.` → `FIVE INTERRUPTIONS TOWARD GOD.` → `A WAVE AROUND THE PLANET.`

segments.voice: Salat is the second pillar of Islam, after the shahada. The five prayers have names, and they follow the sun. Fajr, before dawn. Dhuhr, just after midday. Asr, in the afternoon. Maghrib, just after sunset. Isha, at night. Before praying, Muslims wash in a set way, called wudu: hands, mouth, nose, face, arms, head, ears, feet. Then they face the qibla, the direction of the Kaaba in Mecca. At first the early Muslims faced Jerusalem, and the Qur'an records the change of direction in its second chapter. Each prayer is made of cycles of standing, bowing, prostrating with the forehead on the ground, and sitting, reciting the Qur'an in Arabic, beginning with its opening chapter. Why five? A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari tells of the night journey of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, when fifty daily prayers were first commanded. On the way back, Moses, the story goes, urged him to return and ask for fewer, and he went back again and again until they were five, with the reward of fifty. The Qur'an gives the purpose in a line to Moses himself. In Pickthall's 1930 translation, God says, "establish worship for My remembrance." So the five prayers are, among other things, a way to remember God five times, before the day can make you forget. Practice varies a little. In Shia practice the five prayers are commonly joined into three sessions, and Sunni Muslims may join them when traveling. Mosques call people to each one, but the prayer can be made anywhere clean: an office, a park, an airport floor.

segments.voice: Imagine your day with five pauses in it: waking, midday, afternoon, sunset, bedtime. Rehearse them now, one by one, picturing yourself stopping for a single minute at each. If you pray, that minute can be prayer; if not, a breath, a thank-you, turning your attention toward what matters most.
Salat. The five daily prayers, facing Mecca, from before dawn to after dark: the second pillar of Islam. Today's word.
Your line: five pauses. Five turns toward God, from dawn to dark. That's two hundred sixty-eight days.

269.title: Islam: remembrance
269.hook: in the remembrance of God hearts find rest (Quran 13:28)
269.howItsDone: After the daily prayers Muslims often say subhanallah, alhamdulillah and Allahu akbar on their fingers or prayer beads, and Sufi communities gather for dhikr sessions of chanted remembrance.

segments.voice: Yesterday: salat, the five daily prayers, from before dawn to after dark. Your line was five pauses.

Two in the morning, and a mind that won't stop. It replays the conversation from lunch, rehearses tomorrow's meeting, lists everything that could go wrong. Push the thoughts away and they come back louder. A few hours later, across town, an old man sits in a mosque after the dawn prayer, beads slipping through his fingers, lips moving softly, the same few words again and again. He looks rested. Today: dhikr, remembrance.
screen: `TWO IN THE MORNING, MIND RACING.` → `BEADS AFTER THE DAWN PRAYER.` → `DHIKR.`

segments.voice: Dhikr means remembrance, and also mention: to remember God, and to say God's name. The Qur'an asks for it often. From surah thirteen, in Marmaduke Pickthall's 1930 translation: "Verily in the remembrance of Allah do hearts find rest!" Not by solving everything, but by remembering. Another verse makes it a two-way street: remember me, God says, and I will remember you. The simplest dhikr is short phrases: subhanallah, glory be to God; alhamdulillah, praise be to God; Allahu akbar, God is greater. Hadith reports teach them after the daily prayers, thirty-three times each or close to it, counted on the fingers or on prayer beads called a misbaha or tasbih. And a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari tells that when Fatima, daughter of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, was worn out from hard work and asked for a servant, he taught her to say these same phrases at bedtime, and said they were better for her than a servant. Dhikr can be silent or aloud, alone or together. Among Sufis, the mystical tradition within Islam, groups gather to chant God's names in rhythm, and some Sufi orders pair the words with the breath or with movement. Some keep a quiet dhikr going all day: a phrase at the bus stop, while walking, while falling asleep. The idea is that the heart is always remembering something. Dhikr gives it something that can hold its weight.

segments.voice: Choose a word that settles you: if you're Muslim, it might be Allah or alhamdulillah; if not, peace, or here, or thank you. Say it on each out-breath, silently or softly. When the mind runs off, don't scold it; just come back to the word.
Dhikr. Remembrance: short phrases said again and again, so that, as the Qur'an says, hearts find rest. Today's word.

270.title: Islam: begin with mercy
270.hook: almost every chapter opens: in the name of God, most gracious, most merciful (Quran 1:1)
270.howItsDone: Muslims recite the basmala at the start of each chapter of the Qur'an and say bismillah before eating, traveling, working and many ordinary acts.

segments.voice: Yesterday: dhikr, remembrance, short phrases said again and again. Your line was hearts find rest.

Per my last message. We need to talk. A Monday, begun with a groan. First words set the weather for everything after them. Open a Qur'an to almost any chapter, one hundred thirteen of its one hundred fourteen, and before law or story or warning, the same opening line is waiting. It names God, and then, twice over, it names mercy. Today: Rahman, and the habit of beginning with mercy.
screen: `PER MY LAST MESSAGE.` → `THE SAME FIRST LINE, 113 TIMES.` → `MERCY, TWICE OVER.`

segments.voice: The line is called the basmala, and it opens the very first chapter. In Marmaduke Pickthall's 1930 translation: "In the name of Allah, the Beneficent, the Merciful." In Arabic: bismillah ar-Rahman ar-Rahim. Two names for God, both grown from the same three-letter root, r-h-m. One common reading: Rahman is the vast, overflowing mercy that covers everything and everyone; Rahim is the steady, caring mercy that stays close. The same root gives the Arabic word rahim, the womb. A hadith reports God saying: I am ar-Rahman; I created the womb and gave it a name drawn from my own. The language ties mercy to a mother's love for the child she carries. Another hadith, in Sahih al-Bukhari, says that when God created the world, God wrote: my mercy prevails over my wrath. And another, that God divided mercy into a hundred parts and sent just one down to earth; from that single part, a mother animal lifts her hoof so as not to hurt her young. Only the ninth chapter doesn't open with the basmala, and scholars give different reasons. But the line appears inside chapter twenty-seven, in a letter from Solomon, so the count still comes to one hundred fourteen. Muslims say bismillah before eating, driving, starting work, even entering a room. To begin with God's name is to begin with mercy, before the day's weather is set.

segments.voice: Think of the next thing you'll start, a message, a meeting, a chore, a conversation with someone difficult, and picture its first words. Now soften them: per my last message becomes thanks for this; we need to talk becomes I've been thinking about you. If you pray, you might begin with bismillah.
Rahman. The Most Merciful: mercy that overflows, from the same root as the word for womb, named at the start of almost every chapter. Today's word.
Your line: begin with mercy. Two names, one root, and both of them mercy. See you tomorrow.

271.title: Islam: giving
271.hook: a set share of wealth goes each year to those in need
271.howItsDone: Muslims whose savings exceed the nisab for a lunar year give zakat, usually two and a half percent, directly or through mosques and charities; some pay it in Ramadan, and zakat al-fitr is given before the Eid prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Rahman, the Most Merciful, and the line that opens the chapters. Your line was begin with mercy.

A coin in the cup, when there's one in a pocket. A fundraiser link, tapped because a friend shared it. Giving like that is nice, occasional, optional. Zakat works more like rent. Once a year, a Muslim with enough savings sits down with a calculator, adds them up, and a set share goes to people in need. Not whenever the mood strikes. Every year, on a schedule, as part of the faith.
screen: `A COIN IN THE CUP.` → `A CALCULATOR, ONCE A YEAR.` → `ZAKAT.`

segments.voice: Zakat is the third pillar of Islam, after the shahada and the prayer; in the Qur'an, the command to pray and the command to give zakat often come in the same breath. Here's how it works. If a Muslim's savings stay above a minimum amount, called the nisab, for a full lunar year, they give a portion, by long tradition two and a half percent, to those in need. Islamic law works out the details for gold, crops, livestock and trade goods. The Qur'an names who can receive it, including the poor, the needy, people in debt, travelers stranded far from home, and those working to free captives. Now the word itself. The Qur'an says to the Prophet, in Marmaduke Pickthall's 1930 translation: "Take alms of their wealth, wherewith thou mayst purify them and mayst make them grow." Purify and grow: the two ideas the word zakat carries. And purify them: not the money, the people. Giving cleans the giver's heart of greed and the fear of not having enough. A hadith in Sahih Muslim says charity never decreases wealth. Beside zakat, which is required, there's sadaqah, voluntary giving, which can be anything; a hadith counts even a smile to your brother as sadaqah. Zakat is the floor, set and dependable; sadaqah has no ceiling. Some Muslims time their zakat for Ramadan, and there is a special gift of food before the prayer at the end of Ramadan, so everyone can celebrate.

272.title: Islam: good character
272.hook: Muslims honor the Prophet's gentleness, and a hadith says the best of you are the best in character (Bukhari)
272.howItsDone: Muslims study akhlaq, Islamic ethics, alongside prayer and law, and many learn the Prophet's example of gentleness from the hadith collections and biographies taught in mosques and families.

segments.voice: Yesterday: zakat, the yearly share for those in need. Your line was purified by giving.

The mosque in Medina, the Prophet's own. His companions sit around him. A desert traveler wanders in, a Bedouin who doesn't know the customs, walks to a corner, and starts to relieve himself on the floor. The companions leap up, shouting, ready to drag him out. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, stops them. Let him finish, he says. Then he has a bucket of water poured over the spot, calls the man over, and explains, kindly, what a mosque is for.
screen: `A STRANGER IN THE MOSQUE.` → `THE COMPANIONS LEAP UP.` → `LET HIM FINISH.`

segments.voice: That story is in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, and in one version the Prophet tells his companions: you were sent to make things easy, not to make them difficult. It's one of many. The hadith collections remember his gentleness: mending his own shoes, helping at home, playing with children, standing up when a funeral passed. The Qur'an says to him, in Marmaduke Pickthall's 1930 translation: "And lo! thou art of a tremendous nature." The Arabic word there is khuluq, character, from the same family as akhlaq, the Muslim word for ethics and good conduct. When his wife Aisha was later asked what his character was like, she answered, in a report in Sahih Muslim: his character was the Qur'an. He lived what he recited. And he set character very high. In a hadith in Bukhari, he says: the best of you are those who are best in character. Another says nothing will be heavier on the scale on the Day of Judgment than good character. And another, reported in several collections, has him describe his whole mission as coming to perfect good character. So in Islam, character isn't a pleasant extra added to prayer and fasting. It's what prayer and fasting are for. Tomorrow, that idea reaches even the fast. The Bedouin learned more from the bucket of water than from any shout.

273.title: Ramadan, the fasting month
273.hook: a month of fasting from dawn to sunset, with prayer and generosity (Quran 2:183)
273.howItsDone: During Ramadan adult Muslims who are able fast from dawn to sunset, eat suhur before dawn and break the fast at iftar, often with dates and water, add night prayers, give generously, and celebrate Eid al-Fitr at the end.

segments.voice: Yesterday: good character, and the bucket of water in Medina. Your line was best in character. Today is the last day of the visit to Islam.

A few minutes before sunset in a city apartment. The table is set, but no one's eating: a plate of dates, a jug of water, soup on the stove. The whole family watches the clock, or listens for the call to prayer from the mosque down the street. Nobody has eaten or drunk anything since before dawn, not even a sip of water, and it's been a long, hot day. Then the call comes, someone passes the dates, and a whole city breaks its fast in the same minute.
screen: `DATES, WATER, WATCHING THE CLOCK.` → `NOTHING SINCE BEFORE DAWN.` → `A CITY BREAKS ITS FAST.`

segments.voice: Ramadan is a month of the Islamic calendar, which follows the moon, so it comes a little earlier each year and moves through every season. Fasting in it is the fourth pillar of Islam. The Qur'an gives the command, in Marmaduke Pickthall's 1930 translation: "O ye who believe! Fasting is prescribed for you, even as it was prescribed for those before you, that ye may ward off (evil)." Even as for those before you: the fast stands alongside the fasting of earlier believers. From dawn to sunset, adult Muslims who are able go without food, drink and marital relations. There are exemptions: the sick, travelers, the elderly, those pregnant or nursing, children. A pre-dawn meal, suhur, starts the day; iftar ends it, often with dates and water, as tradition says the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, did. Why this month? The Qur'an says it's the month the Qur'an was sent down, and some aim to recite all of it during the month, with extra night prayers in the mosque. Tradition places in its last ten nights the Night of Power, which the Qur'an calls better than a thousand months. And yesterday's thread returns: a hadith in Bukhari says that if someone fasts but doesn't give up false speech and acting on it, God has no need of their giving up food and drink. The hunger is meant to teach: patience, gratitude, what hunger is like for the poor. The month ends with Eid al-Fitr, a feast. The week, line by line. Shahada: one. Salat: five pauses. Dhikr: hearts find rest. Rahman: begin with mercy. Zakat: purified by giving. Good character: best in character. And Ramadan: hunger teaches.
screen: `A MONTH THAT MOVES WITH THE MOON.` · `FASTING IS PRESCRIBED FOR YOU.` · `THE MONTH THE QUR'AN CAME DOWN.` · `GIVE UP FALSE SPEECH, TOO.` · then, large: `HUNGER TEACHES.`

segments.voice: Notice your body right now: any hunger, any thirst, any restlessness. Don't fix it; just watch it. Then think of someone for whom this feeling isn't chosen and doesn't end at sunset, let the hunger teach you something about them, and if you pray, pray for them.
Ramadan. The month of fasting from dawn to sunset, with prayer, the Qur'an and generosity: the fourth pillar. Today's word.
Your line: hunger teaches. The fast ends in a feast. The week with Islam is complete; tomorrow, Sikhism.
